utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I just make one comment on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness who is protected had some concern about Defence counsel knowing his name. I will explain to the witness that -- we do tell the witnesses that the Defence counsel always gets their name. That's one of the requirements. I didn't see anything that caused me any concern from the question that counsel asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be concrete as regards next week, you said this will be a witness taking us a long time, a long period of time? Just for preparation, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it's 37. While that's being checked, I would say that this witness I think can comment upon many documents. So I've given a list- I don't know if it has been communicated yet to the Court -- excuse me, Witness 35 is the next witness. I think this is a witness that will take more than two days, and it will take at least two days in direct examination if I put all those documents to the witness. I'll proof the witness over the weekend. I'll be meeting with him to see if he can comment on those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observations by the Defence right now on the witnesses, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the witnesses, no, Your Honour. We don't have any observations or comments in connection with that, except for Witness 35, and they did give us, and perhaps this is something that counsel and I can clarify. We do have the transcript from a prior proceeding that seems to stop in the middle of the cross-examination. It stops on page number D7661. And clearly, that's not the end, but I'm sure we can figure that out without your assistance. That would be my only comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this observation. And at the same time, we would ask the OTP, when the Defence is provided with former statements, it's also in the interests of the Bench to have access to these former transcripts. I know the Tribunal runs into serious difficulties when we have the fourth, the fifth, the sixth transcript. And quoting from all the transcripts, but I can't see any solution without infringing the principle of fair trial, this brings me to one reminder I have in my book. I think it was Witness D where the Defence asked for additional transcript. Is this problem resolved right now? There was a

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think it was Witness -- excuse me, I believe it was Witness A, and the Defence was given that after -- actually it was offered it just before the cross-examination, was given to the Defence after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this problem was resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Late, but I guess in the spirit of things, it was resolved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's resolved. Good to know. So whenever there will be in future former transcripts, they should be given not only to the parties, but also to the Bench. But I have to emphasise that there is still also, as regards these transcripts, the obligation under Rule 68 to identify that what the OTP will label as "exculpatory" material. I know it's difficult, but we can't change the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the way I understand Your Honour, is to say that if we provide a transcript, we have to tell the Defence where we believe the witness can help the Defence? Actually, I think that's a broader interpretation of Rule 68 that I have or the case law supports. I understand if we're not providing it, we have to point it out. But if we're providing a whole transcript, I don't think it requires -- I think Dr. Stakic is very well represented and doesn't need any lawyers to give advice as far as what, in a transcript, can help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, as Defence counsel, I would also prefer not to have a document, not in the beginning labelled. But of course, it makes sense that you still have the obligation whenever you find out that something could be exculpatory, for example, exhibits mentioned only this transcript, and you have the impression this could be exculpatory material under 68. So I would say, in dubio, give it to the Defence as such material. I hope there is no disagreement between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I concur with the Court's opinion on that, and we appreciate it if they can identify it for us and provide it to us on a more timely basis, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But coming back to Witness 35, I understood you correctly if you are provided with the additional part of the, you say, missing part of the cross-examination, you're prepared to hear this witness next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's next week, so we're anticipating that our friends across the table will provide us the additional transcripts prior to Friday of this week. And we haven't met with them informally to discuss that, but I am confident they will provide that to us. I do have two other matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think this should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's a problem. Actually, as I recall, that witness was not cross-examined, so I'll double check that, because I don't recall reading any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, just for the record, the cross-examination actually starts and then ends in mid-sentence on the last page. So I think there was further examination of the witness after the questioning by Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that you will both come to an agreement on this, and if not, there will be an opportunity, I think, the last possibility granted to the requesting party was Friday, 11.30. And it can -- I have the confirmation that both parties can live with this date, Friday 11.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's do this. And in addition, also for preparation of Friday, I have to inform the parties that the Bench has decided that it's necessary to have another expert witness, graphologist, on the signature, especially on the one document we got in copy by Mr. Murselovic. And I think this should be discussed on Friday, whether or not such an expert witness has to be heard. As things stand now, it's indispensable for the Bench to have such an expert witness. We all know how difficult it is to have an expert witness on the basis of a photocopy, and this takes a lot of time and a really high-qualified expert. Therefore, we announce this already. If until Friday during the meeting there is no other solution, we will formally order this expert witness to be heard. This is one other point on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My contribution on that is from my 20 years' experience, is that it's very, very difficult- I've almost never seen an identification just from a signature. They usually would require more writing than that. And as Your Honour pointed out, they also would require an original and not a photocopy. So I think it's very unlikely that there be any possibility of a positive identification. And as far as I know, the Defence has not disputed that signature. They have disputed the authenticity of documents with no signature. But I've never heard that they dispute -- I know they don't have to comment on this, the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just your last remark is the reason why I mentioned this today, and we can -- you are prepared to answer the question already? Or do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court would like. My recollection is slightly different than counsel's. We actually did object, if I recall, to the signature of the late Dr. Milan Kovacevic on that. Unlike others that we did object to where there were no signatures, we did specifically object to those signatures because it seemed to us from a layperson again that it was somewhat inconsistent. And I recall specifically counsel offering to the Court that we do have Dr. Kovacevic's original signature because he was incarcerated at the UN Detention Centre in Scheveningen, and we can make a comparison based on that. So I would, at this point, be leaning towards having such an expert on the basis of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, the point was only the document provided, as I probably am wrong, with a signature that was said to be one of Dr. Stakic. And this document was the point of our special concern. The document provided by Mr. Murselovic. If you remember the dispute on the copies, both sides and so on. And this document, this was the basis of our decision that we regard it as necessary, at least to try. And I know there are also limits for these expert witnesses, but to a certain extent, it is possible on the basis of additional material. And as it was pointed out with respect to Mr. Kovacevic, there will be in Scheveningen, additional material available for this comparison. But it's up to the Defence to discuss this with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Objections from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nothing further. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You had two others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just very briefly, if the Court can, at this time, accept the Defence exhibit, the statement that the witness today identified with his signature pages dated September 2nd through 4 of the year 2000, we would like to have the Court accept that as an exhibit. If the Registrar could help us with the next exhibit number, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, let's hear the statement of the OTP. I understand that it's not the content but it's the question when the signature was provided under these -- how many pages? These 17 pages. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Objections from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It should be 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On page 18, I can't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Not the signature of the witness, but the interpreter. It should be 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, you're contesting that the signature was done on the 4th of September, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're not making that contest at this time at all, Judge. What we'd like to do is just enter the exhibit in its entirety after having had the witness identify that it's his signature that appears and he verifies the accuracy of the statement as we discussed during the cross-examination. So we're not arguing as to whether he signed it on the 4th of September, or at any time subsequent to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for better understanding, my point is that when we admitted into evidence one of the previous statements, it was the clear exception, due to the specific circumstances of the signature of these two exhibits at that time. And I think we shouldn't really start -- of course we are open -- but we shouldn't start to admit former exhibits into evidence. We have the contents in our transcripts. There was an examination on this. There was a cross-examination. There were questions by the Judges, and I think this should be in principle enough. If not, you want to say you doubt whether or not the signature was done in the year 2000, September 2 to 4? This should be really the exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Judge, we are not contesting that the signature was or was not done on the date that is reflected on the last pages of the statement. Quite frankly our position is slightly different. We believe that this statement, having been presumably read by the Court, I say it respectfully because it's not necessarily evidence, having read it to compare it with the testimony, and to draw out any potential inconsistencies with the statement may be of assistance in the Defence meeting what we believe is an appropriate Defence and also pointing that the Prosecutor may not have met his burden of proof, if there were certain inconsistencies that go to the threshold issue the counts of the fourth amended indictment. So it is for that purpose that we are seeking this statement as I recall other statements is having been brought in, since the Court has read it and we have asked questions on it, there are other inconsistencies that may have been brought out that we think is necessary for both the briefs at the end of the Prosecutor's case as well as the end of our case that we would like to point out on this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Observations by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the OTP position is, as the questions were put by, I was surprised, because there were no contradictions marked. If it was used for the purpose of marking contradictions, I would have not had any objection. But I object at this stage because there is no purpose. Because the questions have been put to the witness, and he answered the questions, and no contradictions have been marked. So if it's taken in total, I do not see any purpose of the witness coming and giving evidence if you are going to admit this statement. So I see no purpose at this stage if the Defence is not challenging the signature of the witness, and also if there is no other contradictions or inconsistencies marked, there is no basis for the Defence to admit this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As this seems to become a matter of principle, also for future exhibits, I think it's only fair that the Judges deliberate on this and decide on your request tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And your second point was?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Second point is a minor point, and I say this most respectfully to the Tribunal, my co-counsel and lead here, just to the record is clear, and I'm making this purely for the record, Your Honour, we understand your ruling on the issue with respect to the prior "convictions," if I may, without drawing too much into it. But my colleague merely made a point on clarifying the record. We understand your ruling, and we moved from that point immediately. However, the witness seemingly gave an answer, uninvited by us, on an issue, and all we were trying to do at that time was correct the record which didn't seem to reflect the accuracy of the testimony being given by the witness. So I just want the record to be clear, Your Honour, that we were not at any point trying to attempt to expand or go beyond what this Court has ruled on that issue. But as we have in the past, and from time to time unfortunately, we might in the future, we merely just wanted to know if the record was made -- the statement was made by the witness and if the interpreters heard it or not. And the Court can strike it obviously. You can do whatever you wish to do with it. But I just want our position to be clear on that, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As it was discussed already earlier, of course you can test the credibility of a witness. No doubt. But this shouldn't reach a stage where you really could speak about intimidation of a witness. I know that the lines are drawn in a different way in common-law system and in civil-law system. But what we have to do here is to avoid of a clash of these systems, and therefore please understand that we try to find on a case-by-case basis whether it's really worse to be discussed under the headline "credibility" or not. And this was our point here. And we will proceed to have this threshold also in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may, just a last subpart on this second issue, and I do have no more after that, I would like to discuss this issue on prior convictions and the credibility, if I may, with the Court on the Friday, 11.30 meeting, if that would be appropriate, just so the Court knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's already on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could add one point regarding the admission of statements, since Your Honours are going to deliberate regarding that for tomorrow, in my opinion, the offer of the Defence to have these statements admitted for the purpose of seeing whether there were any contradictions with their testimony violates Rule 90 [H] Of the rules of procedure which require that in cross-examination, counsel should put to the witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. That's Rule 90 [H], (ii). The purpose of that rule, and its most fundamental aspect, is unfair to a witness to have them testify, have them leave, go back to their country or wherever they are from, and then argue this statement is contradictory what they testified to without giving the witness an opportunity to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed. This was the underlying reason for our decisions in the past, that we restricted ourselves to only questions when the -- to put it this way, the authenticity of a document was at stake, a signature or whatever. But please, I appreciate to hear your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, I couldn't disagree more with the OTP on this position. If the Court is going to hear the testimony, then the Court should not -- respectfully, the rules don't state that the Court and the Judges will accept an abundance of documents and review them prior to the testimony of the witnesses. Essentially the spirit of the rule was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the Chamber, the Judges, were to take the testimony in. And if we decide to give the statement to the witness to show an inconsistency, we would naturally mark it, identify it, share it with the opposing counsel, the witness, and the Chamber. However, unlike -- nowhere in the rules does it state, the Trial Chamber, not just in this case but in other cases in the past, and certainly will in the future, for efficiency and judicial economy and other unrelated items, have these statements already and are looking at these statements essentially as evidence. So when the judgement or the decisions that are based on evidence, will this panel then ignore all the statements that it has read in the past? Could it ignore all those statements? Those are the critical issues that we have. If this Chamber and the Judges reviewed that, is it evidence? And if it is, all we want to do is mark it as evidence. We have a right under the rules to argue what we perceive as being inconsistent. They can rebut that. The Court could certainly reject our views on that. So I just want to be careful that the record is clear, because the Court itself, if I may say respectfully, I have observed, have read some of the statements. And I don't say it positively or negatively and you have asked questions based on those statements. So I'm just a little concerned that we're putting things to the Court, and maybe this is an issue we can discuss further on Friday. But I totally disagree with counsel's reading of that rule. It's inconsistent with what we're talking about here. There's no basis for that. I think that it's appropriate once the witness identifies a document, says that it's his signature, and we ask that it be introduced. That's the threshold, fundamental authenticity foundation questions that we are required to meet. None more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two questions on this: Would you regard the same as true when it comes to former transcripts? And what about the principle of directness? Isn't it true that a judgement can only be based on that what has been discussed in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's no question the judgement should be based on only that which is discussed in the courtroom. However, what the Court and, at times, the Judges have done is drawn from items that are not in evidence in order to ask questions. The OTP has the burden of proof in this case. And if they failed to ask a question as to what, for example, respectfully, was the disposition or personality or characteristic of Dr. Stakic, a witness may have identified that characteristic in a statement, but it has never been heard in a court. The only other way we can glean as to what that characteristic may be is from an item that is not technically evidence but yet this Court has reviewed and has decided to ask questions upon, therefore making it evidence. So I'm just suggesting, if I may respectfully, again, that if we're going to allow it -- and I don't have an objection to the Court having these statements in advance or the transcripts. If we're going to continue with that process, that the Defence, when they see that a statement is in our interest, what we perceive to be some inconsistencies, whether anyone agrees with that is a totally different issue, but that those documents be admitted intuito as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for these additional observations. Any answer from your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. I think I pointed out Rule 90(H), and counsel didn't contradict that. I stand by the proposed use of the statement to contradict the witness by Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. We have to decide on this tomorrow. Anything else to be decided today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nothing else, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we have to conclude for today. And meet again tomorrow, 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 6.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
